title: Principal component analysis: fewer features, most of the spread
summary: Find the directions along which data varies most, and describe each example by a few coordinates along them.

sources.section: 10.6 Key Steps of PCA in Practice

license: Original work for Python Intelligence; license to be chosen by the owner
objective: Reduce dimensions with principal components and judge how much variance a few components keep.
analogy: PCA turns the camera to the angle where a cloud of points looks widest, then keeps only that view.

misconceptions.belief: PCA works on the raw data as it is.
misconceptions.correction: Centre (and usually scale) the data first; otherwise the first component chases the mean.
They are new directions, combinations of the original features.

misconceptions.belief: The first component explains most of the variance in every dataset.
misconceptions.correction: Sometimes variance is spread out; check the explained-variance ratios.

rubric.evidence: coordinates are dot products with unit component directions
ratios are eigenvalues divided by their total, largest first

review.recall: Why centre data before PCA? What does the explained-variance ratio of a component tell you?

steps.title: Too many features to look at
steps.body:
A table with two features fits on a scatter plot. With fifty, you can't see it, distances get
expensive, and many features repeat each other: a plant's height and stem length rise together.
**Principal component analysis (PCA)** finds a few new directions that keep most of the variation in
the data, so each example can be described by a handful of numbers instead of fifty.

steps.title: The direction of greatest spread
steps.body:
Picture a cloud of points stretched like a cigar. Along its length the points are spread far apart;
across it, hardly at all. Project every point onto the long direction and you keep almost all the
differences between examples with one coordinate. That direction is the **first principal
component**. The second is the direction of greatest remaining spread at right angles to the first,
and so on. Mathematically they are the eigenvectors of the data's covariance matrix, and each
eigenvalue is the variance of the data along its eigenvector.

questions: If every point lies exactly on a line, what is the variance across that line?
Why must the data be centred (mean subtracted) before looking for directions of spread?

steps.title: Watch a point being projected
steps.body: The coordinate of a point along a unit-length direction `u` is the dot product `x · u`. Each frame shows the variables just before the highlighted line runs; the last frame shows what that line printed.

frames.note: 3 × 0.6 + 4 × 0.8: how far the point reaches along u.
The point (3, 4) lies 5 units along u, and nothing across it.

steps.title: The precise rules
steps.body:
**Centre:** subtract each feature's mean, giving `Xc`. (PCA follows variance, and a feature's variance
depends on its units. When features use different units and each should count equally,
standardize them first, as in the scaling lesson.)

**Covariance matrix:** `S = Xcᵀ Xc / N`, a symmetric `D × D` matrix; entry `(i, j)` is the covariance of
features `i` and `j`, and the diagonal holds their variances. In NumPy, `Xc.T` is the transpose and
`@` is matrix multiplication.

**Principal components:** the eigenvectors of `S`, ordered by eigenvalue from largest to smallest.
`np.linalg.eigh(S)` handles symmetric matrices; it returns the eigenvalues in **ascending** order and
the eigenvectors as the **columns** of a matrix, each of length 1. An eigenvector times −1 is still an
eigenvector, so this lesson fixes the sign: the first entry larger than `1e-9` in size is positive.

**Projection:** keep the top `k` components as the rows of `B`; the new coordinates are `Xc @ Bᵀ`,
one row of `k` numbers per example.

**Explained variance:** component `i` explains `λᵢ / (λ₁ + … + λ_D)` of the total variance; the
ratios of all `D` components add up to 1.

steps.title: Run it: one direction holds almost everything
steps.body: Six points close to a straight line. Predict roughly what share of the variance the first component explains.
steps.code:
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[1.0, 1.2], [2.0, 1.9], [3.0, 3.2], [4.0, 3.8], [5.0, 5.1], [6.0, 5.8]])
mean = X.mean(axis=0)
Xc = X - mean
S = Xc.T @ Xc / len(X)
print(np.round(S, 3))

values, vectors = np.linalg.eigh(S)
order = np.argsort(values)[::-1]
values, vectors = values[order], vectors[:, order]
print(np.round(values, 3))
print(np.round(values / values.sum(), 4))

u = vectors[:, 0]
if u[np.argmax(np.abs(u) > 1e-9)] < 0:
    u = -u
print(np.round(u, 3))
print(np.round(Xc @ u, 2))

steps.title: Your turn: the covariance matrix
steps.body:
Complete `covariance_matrix(X)`: centre each column of `X` on its mean, then return `Xcᵀ Xc / N` as a
list of lists of floats (`N` is the number of rows). Raise `ValueError` if `X` has no rows, and don't
change `X`.
hints: `A - A.mean(axis=0)` centres every column at once.
With the centred array `C`, `C.T @ C` is a `D × D` matrix; divide it by the number of rows.

tests.name: two features
tests.code:
got = covariance_matrix([[1, 2], [3, 6], [5, 4]])
want = [[8 / 3, 4 / 3], [4 / 3, 8 / 3]]
assert all(abs(a - b) < 1e-12 for gr, wr in zip(got, want) for a, b in zip(gr, wr)) and [len(r) for r in got] == [2, 2], f'expected about {want}; got {got}'

tests.name: matches NumPy (dividing by N)
tests.code:
import numpy as np
X = [[0.5, 1.0, -2.0], [1.5, 0.0, 4.0], [2.0, 3.0, 1.0], [7.0, -1.0, 0.25]]
got = np.array(covariance_matrix(X))
want = np.cov(np.array(X).T, bias=True)
assert got.shape == (3, 3) and np.allclose(got, want, rtol=0, atol=1e-12), f'divide by N (bias=True), not N - 1; got {got.tolist()}'

tests.name: variances on the diagonal
tests.code:
got = covariance_matrix([[2, 10], [4, 10], [6, 10]])
assert abs(got[0][0] - 8 / 3) < 1e-12 and got[1][1] == 0.0 and got[0][1] == got[1][0] == 0.0, f'a constant column has variance 0 and covariance 0; got {got}'

tests.name: a single feature
tests.code:
got = covariance_matrix([[1], [3], [5]])
assert type(got) is list and len(got) == 1 and type(got[0]) is list and len(got[0]) == 1 and abs(got[0][0] - 8 / 3) < 1e-12, f'one feature gives a 1 x 1 matrix [[8/3]], still a list of lists; got {got!r}'

tests.name: one row
tests.code:
got = covariance_matrix([[3, 4, 5]])
assert got == [[0.0] * 3] * 3, 'a single row has no spread'
assert type(got) is list and all(type(r) is list and all(isinstance(v, float) for v in r) for r in got), 'a list of lists of floats'

tests.name: plain lists of floats
tests.code:
got = covariance_matrix([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
assert type(got) is list and all(type(r) is list for r in got) and all(isinstance(v, float) for r in got for v in r), 'return a list of lists of floats'

tests.name: X is not changed
tests.code:
X = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
covariance_matrix(X)
assert X == [[1, 2], [3, 4]], 'do not modify X'
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1.5, 2.0], [3.0, 7.0], [0.5, 1.0]])
saved = A.copy()
covariance_matrix(A)
assert np.array_equal(A, saved), 'do not modify a NumPy array passed as X either (np.asarray shares its memory)'

tests.name: no rows

steps.title: Challenge: PCA from scratch
steps.body:
The starter gives you `covariance_matrix`. Write `pca_fit(X, k)`, which returns a dictionary with
`'mean'` (the column means), `'components'` (the top `k` eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, largest
eigenvalue first, each a list with the sign rule above), `'variances'` (their eigenvalues) and
`'explained'` (each eigenvalue divided by the sum of **all** eigenvalues). Raise `ValueError` if `X`
has no rows, if `k` is not between 1 and the number of features, or if the data has no spread (every
row identical; compare the rows, since rounding can leave a tiny variance).
Then write `pca_transform(model, X)`, which centres new rows with the model's **stored** mean and
returns their coordinates along the components (one list of `k` floats per row; `[]` for no rows).
You may assume the eigenvalues you keep are all different.
hints: `values, vectors = np.linalg.eigh(S)`, then `order = np.argsort(values)[::-1]` sorts from largest; reorder both, taking `vectors[:, order]` (columns!).
For the sign rule, `u[np.argmax(np.abs(u) > 1e-9)]` is the first entry larger than `1e-9` in size; if it is negative, use `-u`.

tests.name: components along the axes
tests.code:
X = [[3, 0, 0], [-3, 0, 0], [0, 2, 0], [0, -2, 0], [0, 0, 1], [0, 0, -1]]
close = lambda a, b: len(a) == len(b) and all(abs(x - y) < 1e-9 for x, y in zip(a, b))
model = pca_fit(X, 3)
assert len(model['components']) == 3 and all(close(c, w) for c, w in zip(model['components'], [[1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1]])), f'the spread is largest along x, then y, then z; got {model["components"]}'
assert close(model['variances'], [3, 4 / 3, 1 / 3]), f'variances 18/6, 8/6, 2/6; got {model["variances"]}'
assert close(model['explained'], [9 / 14, 4 / 14, 1 / 14]) and close(model['mean'], [0, 0, 0])

tests.name: largest variance first, whatever the column order
tests.code:
X = [[0, 0, 1], [0, 0, -1], [0, 5, 0], [0, -5, 0], [2, 0, 0], [-2, 0, 0]]
close = lambda a, b: len(a) == len(b) and all(abs(x - y) < 1e-9 for x, y in zip(a, b))
model = pca_fit(X, 2)
assert len(model['components']) == 2 and close(model['components'][0], [0, 1, 0]) and close(model['components'][1], [1, 0, 0]), f'y spreads most, then x; got {model["components"]}'
assert close(model['variances'], [25 / 3, 4 / 3]) and close(model['explained'], [25 / 30, 4 / 30]), f'explained divides by the sum of ALL variances (30/3); got {model}'

tests.name: the sign rule
tests.code:
close = lambda a, b: len(a) == len(b) and all(abs(x - y) < 1e-9 for x, y in zip(a, b))
model = pca_fit([[1, 1], [2, 2], [3, 3], [1, 1.5]], 1)
u = model['components'][0]
assert u[0] > 0 and abs(sum(v * v for v in u) - 1) < 1e-9, f'unit length, first entry positive; got {u}'
model = pca_fit([[0, 1, -1], [0, -1, 1], [0, 2, -2], [0, -2, 2.5]], 1)
u = model['components'][0]
assert abs(u[0]) < 1e-9 and u[1] > 0 and u[2] < 0, f'the first entry is 0, so the second decides the sign; got {u}'
model = pca_fit([[t * 1e-10, -t] for t in (-2.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0)], 1)
u = model['components'][0]
assert u[1] > 0 and u[0] < 0 and abs(u[0]) < 1e-9, f'the first entry (about 1e-10) is below the 1e-9 threshold, so the second entry decides; got {u}'
got = pca_transform(model, [[0, -3]])
assert abs(got[0][0] + 3) < 1e-9, f'(0, -3) lies 3 units against the component; got {got}'

tests.name: a correlated cloud
tests.code:
import numpy as np
X = [[1.0, 1.2], [2.0, 1.9], [3.0, 3.2], [4.0, 3.8], [5.0, 5.1], [6.0, 5.8]]
close = lambda a, b: len(a) == len(b) and all(abs(x - y) < 1e-9 for x, y in zip(a, b))
A = np.array(X)
C = A - A.mean(axis=0)
S = C.T @ C / len(A)
vals, vecs = np.linalg.eigh(S)
u = vecs[:, 1] if vecs[0, 1] > 0 else -vecs[:, 1]
model = pca_fit(X, 1)
assert close(model['components'][0], u.tolist()), f'expected about {u.tolist()}; got {model["components"]}'
assert close(model['variances'], [vals[1]]) and close(model['explained'], [vals[1] / vals.sum()])
got = pca_transform(model, X)
assert len(got) == 6 and all(len(r) == 1 for r in got) and close([r[0] for r in got], (C @ u).tolist()), f'coordinates along u; got {got}'

tests.name: every component of a correlated 3-D cloud
tests.code:
import numpy as np
X = [[2.0, 1.0, 0.5], [3.5, 2.5, 1.0], [1.0, 0.0, 2.0], [4.0, 3.5, -1.0], [2.5, 2.0, 0.0], [5.0, 3.0, 1.5], [0.5, 1.5, 0.5]]
close = lambda a, b: len(a) == len(b) and all(abs(x - y) < 1e-9 for x, y in zip(a, b))
A = np.array(X)
C = A - A.mean(axis=0)
vals, vecs = np.linalg.eigh(C.T @ C / len(A))
order = np.argsort(vals)[::-1]
vals, vecs = vals[order], vecs[:, order]
assert len(set(np.round(vals, 6))) == 3
want = []
for j in range(3):
    u = vecs[:, j]
    want.append((-u if u[np.argmax(np.abs(u) > 1e-9)] < 0 else u).tolist())
model = pca_fit(X, 3)
assert len(model['components']) == 3 and all(close(c, w) for c, w in zip(model['components'], want)), f'every component, in order, with the sign rule: expected about {want}; got {model["components"]}'
assert close(model['variances'], vals.tolist()) and close(model['explained'], (vals / vals.sum()).tolist())
got = pca_transform(model, X)
B = np.array(want)
assert type(got) is list and len(got) == 7 and all(close(r, w) for r, w in zip(got, (C @ B.T).tolist())), f'coordinates along all three components; got {got}'
two = pca_fit(X, 2)
assert len(two['components']) == 2 and all(close(c, w) for c, w in zip(two['components'], want[:2]))
got2 = pca_transform(two, X)
want2 = (C @ np.array(want[:2]).T).tolist()
assert type(got2) is list and len(got2) == 7 and all(close(r, w) for r, w in zip(got2, want2)), f'coordinates along the top two components; got {got2}'

tests.name: a single feature
tests.code:
close = lambda a, b: len(a) == len(b) and all(abs(x - y) < 1e-9 for x, y in zip(a, b))
model = pca_fit([[1], [3], [5]], 1)
assert close(model['components'][0], [1.0]) and close(model['variances'], [8 / 3]) and close(model['explained'], [1.0]) and close(model['mean'], [3.0]), f'one feature: the only component is (1); got {model}'
got = pca_transform(model, [[7], [3]])
assert type(got) is list and len(got) == 2 and close(got[0], [4.0]) and close(got[1], [0.0]), f'got {got}'

tests.name: new rows use the stored mean
tests.code:
X = [[3, 0, 0], [-3, 0, 0], [0, 2, 0], [0, -2, 0], [0, 0, 1], [0, 0, -1]]
close = lambda a, b: len(a) == len(b) and all(abs(x - y) < 1e-9 for x, y in zip(a, b))
model = pca_fit(X, 2)
got = pca_transform(model, [[1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3]])
assert len(got) == 2 and all(close(r, [1, 2]) for r in got), f'centre with the training mean (0, 0, 0), not the new rows\' mean; got {got}'
shifted = pca_fit([[x + 10, y, z] for x, y, z in X], 1)
assert close(shifted['mean'], [10, 0, 0]) and close(pca_transform(shifted, [[13, 5, 5]])[0], [3]), 'subtract the stored mean before projecting'

tests.name: one row and no rows
tests.code:
X = [[3, 0, 0], [-3, 0, 0], [0, 2, 0], [0, -2, 0], [0, 0, 1], [0, 0, -1]]
model = pca_fit(X, 2)
assert pca_transform(model, []) == [], 'no rows in, no rows out'
close = lambda a, b: len(a) == len(b) and all(abs(x - y) < 1e-9 for x, y in zip(a, b))
got = pca_transform(model, [[0, -2, 0]])
assert type(got) is list and len(got) == 1 and close(got[0], [0, -2]), f'a list with one row; got {got!r}'

tests.name: plain lists of floats
tests.code:
X = [[3, 0, 0], [-3, 0, 0], [0, 2, 0], [0, -2, 0], [0, 0, 1], [0, 0, -1]]
model = pca_fit(X, 2)
assert set(model) == {'mean', 'components', 'variances', 'explained'}, f'keys mean, components, variances, explained; got {sorted(model)}'
for v in [model['mean'], model['variances'], model['explained'], *model['components'], *pca_transform(model, X)]:
    assert type(v) is list and all(isinstance(t, float) for t in v), f'plain lists of floats; got {v!r}'
assert type(model['components']) is list

tests.name: inputs are not changed
tests.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1.5, 2.0], [3.0, 7.0], [0.5, 1.0]])
saved = A.copy()
model = pca_fit(A, 1)
assert np.array_equal(A, saved), 'pca_fit must not modify X'
B = np.array([[2.0, 3.0]])
keep = B.copy()
pca_transform(model, B)
assert np.array_equal(B, keep), 'pca_transform must not modify X'
import copy
X = [[1.5, 2.0], [3.0, 7.0], [0.5, 1.0]]
keep_X = copy.deepcopy(X)
model = pca_fit(X, 1)
assert X == keep_X, 'pca_fit must not modify a list of lists'
new = [[2.0, 3.0], [9.0, -1.0]]
keep_new = copy.deepcopy(new)
pca_transform(model, new)
assert new == keep_new, 'pca_transform must not modify a list of lists (the stored mean is not zero here)'

tests.name: bad input

steps.title: Transfer: projecting and keeping enough variance
steps.body:
Write `project(X, components)`: centre the rows of X by their column means and return their coordinates along each
component (components is a (k, d) array of unit vectors). Then write `components_needed(eigenvalues, share)`: the
smallest number of components (taken largest eigenvalue first) whose explained-variance ratios add up to at least `share`.
hints: Sort descending, divide by the total, take the running sum with `np.cumsum`, and find the first position reaching `share`.

tests.name: centres, then projects
tests.code:
import numpy as np
X = np.array([[1.0, 1.0], [3.0, 3.0]])
Z = project(X, np.array([[1.0, 1.0]]) / np.sqrt(2))
assert np.allclose(Z, [[-np.sqrt(2)], [np.sqrt(2)]]), Z

tests.name: several components
tests.code:
import numpy as np
X = np.array([[2.0, 0.0], [0.0, 4.0], [4.0, 2.0]])
Z = project(X, np.eye(2))
assert Z.shape == (3, 2) and np.allclose(Z.mean(axis=0), 0)
C = np.array([[1.0, -1.0], [1.0, 1.0]]) / np.sqrt(2)
r = np.sqrt(2)
assert np.allclose(project(X, C), [[r, -r], [-2 * r, 0.0], [r, r]]), 'keep each component as given, signs included'

tests.name: components needed for a share of variance
tests.code:
assert components_needed([1.0, 6.0, 3.0], 0.6) == 1 and components_needed([1.0, 6.0, 3.0], 0.85) == 2
assert components_needed([5.0, 5.0], 1.0) == 2

tests.name: fractional column means, with integer input too
tests.code:
import numpy as np
X = np.array([[1, 2], [2, 4], [4, 5]])
expected = X - np.array([7 / 3, 11 / 3])
assert np.allclose(project(X, np.eye(2)), expected) and np.allclose(project(X.astype(float), np.eye(2)), expected)

tests.name: shares just past a boundary
tests.code: assert components_needed([6.0, 3.0, 1.0], 0.61) == 2 and components_needed([6.0, 3.0, 1.0], 0.91) == 3

questions.prompt: The eigenvalues of a covariance matrix are 6, 3 and 1. What share of the variance do the first two components explain?
`np.linalg.eigh` returns eigenvalues `[0.5, 2.0, 7.5]`. Which column of the eigenvector matrix is the first principal component?
questions.explanation: eigh sorts eigenvalues in ascending order, so the largest, 7.5, is last; eigenvectors are columns.

questions.prompt: A dataset has 10 features. What is the largest number of principal components it can have?
choices: As many as there are examples
questions.explanation: One component per dimension of the feature space: the covariance matrix is 10 × 10.

questions.prompt: Your features are in different units (metres, seconds, ratios) and each should count equally. What should you do before PCA?
choices: Drop the features with small values
questions.explanation: Variance depends on units, so without standardizing a feature can dominate just because of how it was measured.

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.body:
- Explain principal components as the directions of greatest spread, and eigenvalues as the variance along them.
- Compute a covariance matrix and its eigenvectors with NumPy, in the right order and with a fixed sign.
- Project new examples onto the top components using the stored training mean.
- Report how much of the variance a few components explain.
